extracted.intended_audience: schoolchildren and elementary-school teachers (18th‑century English grammar learners)
extracted.subtask_description: A late‑18th‑century elementary grammar textbook laying out rules and teaching guidance for spelling, pronunciation, parts of speech, inflection, agreement (concord), punctuation, and style aimed at young learners. Contains definitions, rules, examples, and lists (including many irregular verbs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of grammar into four parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar is commonly divided into four parts: Orthography, Etymology, Syntax, and Prosody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orthography teaches the true spelling of words; Etymology treats the different kinds of words, their derivations and variations; Syntax teaches how to join words together in a sentence; Prosody teaches rules of pronunciation and versification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthography (spelling & alphabet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthography teaches the true spelling of words and begins with the English alphabet and the classification of letters into vowels and consonants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alphabet consists of 26 letters. A vowel 'has a full and perfect sound of itself' (listed as a, e, i, o, u, w, y); consonants 'have no sound unless when joined to a vowel' (nineteen listed). Guidance includes which letters are vowels and consonants and the basic function of each class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter‑sound rules (hard/soft and silent letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules describing when letters have hard or soft sounds and when letters are silent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C sounds hard like k before a, o, u, l, r and at ends; C sounds soft like s before e, i, y. G has hard and soft sounds (hard before a, o, u, l, r and at ends; soft like j before e, i, y). G is silent before n and m at ends of words. W is silent before r. 'Ch' sometimes sounds like k or like sh; 'Ph' sounds like f; letter groups 'ci', 'si', 'ti' before a vowel generally sound like sh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllable, diphthong, triphthong
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of syllable and diphthong/triphthong and enumeration of diphthongs in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A syllable is the sound of one or more letters pronounced by one impulse of breath; there are as many syllables as distinct sounds. A diphthong is the sound of two vowels in one syllable. The book lists twenty diphthongs (aa, ai, au, aw, ay, ea, ee, ei, eo, eu, ew, ey, ie, oa, oi, oo, ou, ow, oy, ui). A triphthong is the sound of three vowels in one syllable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stops / punctuation and reading pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: List of reading stops (punctuation marks) and the amount of pause to observe when reading aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stops: Comma, Semicolon, Colon, Period, Interrogation (?), Exclamation (!). A comma stops the voice for a count of 1; semicolon 1–2; colon 1–2–3; period/interrogation/exclamation 1–2–3–4. Detailed uses: comma after every distinct number of words or figures, after each adjective belonging to the same substantive except the last, after names of persons called upon, after distinct clause of a sentence; semicolon before causal and exceptive conjunctions (for, because, but, &c.) and to distinguish contrarieties; colon used after a score not entirely complete and before comparative conjunctions in similitude; period used at the end of a complete sentence; interrogation after a question; exclamation when something is admired or exclaimed against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of typographical/diacritical marks
rubrics_metrics.description: List of marks used in printing/reading and their names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes Accent, Paragraph, Apostrophe, Crotchet, Asterisk, Parenthesis, Breve, Quotation, Caret, Diæresis, Circumflex (Section), Hyphen, Ellipses, Index (Brace), Obelisk, etc. (as listed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Directions for capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for when to use capital letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the first letter of every book, chapter, paragraph, writing, every line of poetry, after a Period, Colon, Interrogation, and Exclamation. Capitalize titles of the Divinity, proper names of persons/places/things, titles of men and women, arts and sciences, trades, national adjectives. A notable saying or quoted passage begins with a capital. The pronoun I and the interjection O are always capitals. Capitals may be used ornamentally in titles or whole words/sentences for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etymology / parts of speech (ten kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are ten kinds of words or parts of speech in the English language: Article, Substantive (Noun), Pronoun, Adjective, Verb, Participle, Adverb, Preposition, Conjunction, Interjection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part of speech is briefly defined: Article (limits a substantive); Substantive (name of person/place/thing); Pronoun (used instead of a noun); Adjective (denotes a property of its substantive); Verb (chief word signifying acting or being); Participle (derived from a verb with nature of verb and adjective); Adverb (joined to verb/participle/adjective/another adverb to express quality or circumstance); Preposition (connects nouns/pronouns and shows relation); Conjunction (connects/join words and sentences); Interjection (expresses sudden emotion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles (a, an, the) — usage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Three articles: a, an, and the, with rules for their use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 'a' is used before words beginning with a consonant; 'an' before words beginning with a vowel or silent h. 'A' and 'an' are placed before substantives of the singular number only. 'The' determines what particular person or thing is meant and may be placed before singular and plural substantives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantives (nouns): proper/common, number, person, case, gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Nouns are proper or common; they have number, person, case, and gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper substantive names any particular person/place/thing; common names things in general. Number: singular and plural (plural generally formed by adding s or es). Persons: first/second/third in each number (definitions given). Cases: Nominative (before verb), Genitive (has the sign 's), Dative (signs to/for), Accusative (follows the verb), Vocative (calls/speaks to), Ablative (signs in, with, through, from, by, than). Gender: masculine (males), feminine (females), neuter (neither).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns: kinds and declension
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns are of six kinds: Personal, Demonstrative, Possessive, Definitive, Relative, Distributive; personal pronouns are declined by person/number and have leading/following states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal pronouns examples and declensions given (I/me, thou/thee, he/him, we/us, ye/you, they/them). Possessive pronouns listed (my, thy, his, her, our, your, their) and full forms (mine, thine, ours, yours, theirs). Relative pronouns (who, which, what, whether, whose) and note that 'who' used for persons, 'which' for things. Demonstrative pronouns 'this'/'that' (this→these; that→those). Definitive pronouns (other, any, none, some, one). Distributive pronouns (each, every, either). Guidance: when 'that' is demonstrative vs conjunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives and degrees of comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives vary only to express comparison: positive, comparative, superlative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive expresses quality without increase/decrease. Comparative somewhat increases/decreases positive and formed by adding -er/-r or putting 'more' before it. Superlative increases/decreases to the utmost and is formed by adding -est or putting 'most' before it. Irregular comparisons listed (good→better→best; bad→worse→worst; much/many→more→most; near→nearer→nearest or next, late→later→latest or last).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbs: active and neuter; chief properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbs are active (denote doing) or neuter (denote existing/being in some posture). Chief properties: mode, tense, number, person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A verb is identified by whether 'to' or a personal pronoun can be prefixed; modes and tenses are described in other rules; verbs must agree with their nominative in number and person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb modes (Infinitive, Indicative, Imperative, Potential, Subjunctive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five modes: Infinitive (no number/person; known by 'to'), Indicative (declares or asks), Imperative (commands/entreats; sign 'let'), Potential (expresses ability/necessity/permission; signs: may, can, must, might, could, would, should), Subjunctive (conditional; usually proceeds by 'if' or other conditional conjunction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicative signs: do, did, have, had, shall, will. Imperative sign 'Let'. Potential and Subjunctive explained with examples and conjugations shown in tables for various tenses/modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb tenses (present, imperfect, perfect, preterpluperfect, future)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five tenses distinguished by time and signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present indicated by do, dost, doth, does; Imperfect (past, not finished) by did/didst; Perfect (action completely finished) by have/has/hath; Preterpluperfect (action finished before a certain past time) by had/hadst; Future by shall/will. Conjugation examples for 'to be' and other verbs are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helping verbs (auxiliaries) — list and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain verbs join to other verbs to fix mode and tense with greater exactness; these are called helping verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helping verbs listed: do, did, have, had, shall, will, may, can, must, might, could, would, should, etc. They form compound tenses (perfect, future, potential) and are conjugated according to person and number (tables provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugation practice and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugation of verbs through modes/tenses/numbers shown by paradigms (e.g., 'to be', 'to learn', 'to drink').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive conjugation tables provided for 'to be', 'to learn', 'to drink' across modes (Infinitive, Indicative, Imperfect, Perfect, Pluperfect, Futures, Imperative, Potential, Subjunctive) and examples of usage in sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential (modal) usage and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential mode attaches power, liberty, will, duty, or necessity to the verb and has specific signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs: may, can, must, might, could, would, should; tables provided for present, imperfect, perfect, preterpluperfect forms with examples like 'I may or can be', 'I must, might, could, would, or should have been'. Future often expressed by present 'I may or can go to‑morrow.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjunctive forms and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjunctive is conditional and used after conditional conjunctions (if, though).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Present subjunctive 'If I be, if thou be...'; Imperfect subjunctive 'Though I were, though thou wert...'; tables show forms and compound tenses in subjunctive mood for various verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular verbs — identification and list
rubrics_metrics.description: Irregular verbs are those which do not form their perfect tense and passive participle in -ed; the book provides an alphabetical list of irregular verbs with present, imperfect, and participle forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large alphabetical listing of irregular verbs with their imperfect and participle forms is provided; note that some verbs marked with 'x' have both regular and irregular forms in use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participles: active and passive (formation and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of participles: active (ending in -ing) and passive (ending in -ed, -t, or -n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active formed by adding -ing to the present infinitive (dropping final e if present). Passive participle in regular verbs formed by adding -ed or -d; passive participle must be used with helping verbs to form perfect and pluperfect tenses. Examples and infinitive/participle pairs given (To love → Loving; To love → Loved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs — formation and questions answered
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs generally end in -ly and answer questions such as How? How much? When? Where?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mercifully, foolishly, only; long lists of common adverbs and adverbial words (now, since, to‑morrow, to‑day, ago, oft, already, yesterday, before, hereafter, often, hitherto, henceforth, soon, seldom, always, when, then, never, here, there, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepositions — principal list and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal prepositions listed and defined as words put before nouns/pronouns to show relation and to connect them with other words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepositions include above, about, after, against, along, among, between, concerning, during, for, from, in, into, near, nigh, out, on, over, since, through, till, to, towards, upon, until, unto, under, with, within, without, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunctions — list and connective function
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of conjunctions that connect like states of pronouns and the same mode and tense of verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjunctions enumerated include again, for, since, albeit, however, so, also, than, although, likewise, therefore, and, moreover, thereupon, as, neither, though, because, nevertheless, unless, both, nor, whereas, but, notwithstanding, whereupon, either...or, whether, else, otherwise, yet, except, save, that, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE I
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule I: A verb must agree with its Nominative word in number and person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic agreement principle; many examples and incorrect‑correct contrasts appear later under 'Examples under all the foregoing rules.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE II
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule II: Two or more nouns or pronouns joined together by a copulative conjunction require verbs, nouns, and pronouns agreeing with them in the plural number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subjects are connected by 'and', plural agreement is required. Examples in book show common errors and correct forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE III
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule III: Nouns of number or multitude may have the verb or pronoun in the singular or plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective nouns may take singular or plural agreement depending on sense; examples like 'the parliament are' vs 'the parliament is' illustrate optional agreement depending on emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE IV
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule IV: The verbs 'am' and 'was' have the leading state of a pronoun both before and after them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on forms like 'I am he' and explains pronoun case before/after 'to be'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE V
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule V: The pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number, gender, and person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard pronoun‑antecedent agreement rule; illustrative examples given throughout the examples section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE VI
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule VI: When a pronoun comes before the verb it must be of the leading state; when set after the verb it must be of the following state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance about using subject (leading) vs object (following) pronoun forms relative to verb position; many erroneous example sentences illustrate mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE VII
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule VII: When there is a nominative case between the pronoun and the verb, the pronoun must be of the following state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains use of objective/subjective pronouns when intervening nominative occurs; examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE VIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule VIII: The pronouns 'this' and 'that' must agree with their substantives in number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: 'This makes these' in plural, 'That makes those', usage notes clarifying demonstratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule IX: A preposition has the following state (objective) of a pronoun after it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective pronoun after prepositions: 'to whom', 'with whom', etc.; numerous example sentences show misuse to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE X
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule X: When two substantives come together, the first is turned into the genitive case by adding 's to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on possessive formation: 'Robert's book', 'the king's picture', 'John's copy is well written', with examples of correct usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE XI
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule XI: Conjunctions connect like states of pronouns and the same mode and tense of verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to keep grammatical forms parallel when joined by conjunctions (e.g., do not mix different cases or tenses across joined elements). Examples show common violations and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE XII
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule XII: The comparative adverbs 'more' and 'most' must not be set before adjectives compared by -er and -est.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid doubling comparative markers: incorrect 'more better' or 'most beft' are cited as errors; use either -er/-est or more/most appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE XIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule XIII: The genitive case of 'who' (whose) should only be used when it relates to persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'whose' for persons primarily; the book notes improper uses and shows correct constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE XIV
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule XIV: In imperative and interrogative sentences the nominative case follows the principal verb or the auxiliary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains forms like 'Hear ye' and old/formal imperatives 'Go thou', 'Learn thou' and questions where nominative follows verb in classical constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for English Concord — RULE XV
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule XV: When two or more nouns equally related to a verb are connected by a disjunctive conjunction, and equally related to a verb, the verb agrees best with the nearest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains agreement in subjects joined by 'or'/'nor' and advises agreement with the noun nearest the verb (examples: Neither the pens nor the ruler is here; when reversed, agreement changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical guidance: concise definitions for children
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefatory guidance that children 'whose memories are in general very weak' should not be loaded with a multiplicity of words; shorter definitions are better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book was drawn up to remove difficulties children meet from long and tedious definitions and to lead them imperceptibly into knowledge of first principles; method intended for use in the author's own school and obvious to discerning teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthographic conventions and common error examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout, many erroneous example sentences are given to illustrate nonstandard or incorrect usage (concord errors, verb forms, pronoun cases, comparative mistakes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples serve as anti‑patterns: e.g., 'I is sick', 'He art sleeping', 'We does sing', 'John and James was first at school', 'more better', 'that boys are playing' — these illustrate what to avoid and provide corrective contexts.
